| [LIT-130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md) v2 | Personal Identity and Ethics | Dufner (2025), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/identity-ethics/>. A survey, arguing no thesis of its own, of how three contested questions bear on ethics: which account of persistence is true (unique psychological continuity, Shoemaker and Parfit; or biological continuity and animalism, Olson and DeGrazia), whether identity or the psychological relations (continuity and/or connectedness) is what matters (Parfit's fission case), and whether metaphysics constrains ethics or the reverse. | [LIT-139](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md) v2 | Inductive Risk and Values in Science | Douglas (2000), DOI-10.1086/392855. Hempel's "inductive risk" (the chance of wrongly accepting or rejecting a hypothesis) arises at three internal stages of science: choosing a methodology such as a significance level, characterising data, and interpreting results. Wherever the non-epistemic consequences of error can be foreseen, weighing them requires non-epistemic values. Douglas shows this on dioxin cancer studies. Three pathologist panels (1978, 1980, 1990) scored the same Kociba rat-liver slides differently (e.g. 34/50, 33/47, 18/50 tumours at 100 ng/kg/day). Choosing between threshold and no-threshold readings of the same data has meant regulatory limits about 100× apart. Values enter only indirectly, through the consequences of error, never as evidence that a claim is true. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-145.md)); worth reading as the canonical, compact statement of the modern inductive-risk argument. It is carefully scoped, with an explicit direct/indirect distinction and exemptions for negligible uncertainty and consequence-free research, and it is well illustrated. Its normative premise, that scientists bear moral responsibility for foreseeable consequences of error, is explicitly left unargued (§2, p. 563). |
| [LIT-146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-146.md) v2 | The Moral Status of Animals | Gruen & Monsó (2003), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/moral-animal/>. The entry reviews five proposed grounds of moral considerability (species membership, human-exceptional capacities, personhood, sentience and agency). Its conclusion is that attempts to establish human uniqueness by capacities are "not the most promising" (§1.2). It then separates *having* moral status from the *weight* of a claim ("showing up on a moral radar screen", §2.2). Weight depends on the value theory adopted for animal interests (hedonism, preference satisfaction, objective list; §2.1) and on the normative framework (rights, which are absolute but generate forward-looking duties when violated, or a multi-factor utilitarianism). It closes with virtue-ethical, feminist, relational and empathy-based approaches that reject argument from capacities altogether (§3). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md)); worth reading as the standard current survey of the grounds and weighing of animals' moral status. The paper proposes, without implementation, formalism or experiment, that an AI system which designs further AI systems should pass on one "immutable" principle. The principle is: do not directly harm humanity or violate fundamental human values; monitor and mitigate misuse of your outputs; and make every derivative inherit this principle (p. 12). The mechanisms are a genetic-algorithm analogy, with immutable and mutable "genes", constrained crossover and filtered mutation, together with "temporal cloning". The paper is inconsistent about its central notion. The principle is enforced once by a penalty F = Q − α·P (p. 9) and once by "unbreachable" hard constraints (p. 13). | [LIT-189](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-189.md) v2 | Philosophy of Open Science | Leonelli (2023), DOI-10.1017/9781009416368. Leonelli argues that mainstream, institutional Open Science treats openness as the unlimited, digital sharing of research objects, a transparency-first ordering running transparency → quality (reproducibility) → inclusion. This rests on an object-oriented, "resourcist" epistemology of science. Four implementation cases (GISAID COVID data, open-source software stigma, crop-data linkage, the reproducibility "crisis") show it can narrow epistemic diversity and entrench epistemic injustice, which lowers reliability. Against two beliefs, that every question about personal identity must have an answer and that important questions turn on it. In Wiggins's division case, each half-brain recipient stands in the relation that would be survival if there were only one, so "how could a double success be a failure?". What matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can branch and come in degrees, while identity is one-one and all-or-nothing. Q-memory and q-intention show the relations need not presuppose identity. Speaking of past and future selves by degree of connectedness, the principle of self-interest has no independent force. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md)), in a JSTOR copy of the published article posted on a University of Athens course page; worth reading as the paper that separated what matters in survival from identity, and the short original of Part III of Reasons and Persons. Its division case makes "I survive as neither" absurd and "I survive as both" incompatible with identity, so it concludes that what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can branch and come in degrees, while identity cannot. It supplies q-memory, the non-branching criterion, and the vocabulary of successive selves. Its first conclusion is argued; its claim that connectedness matters more than continuity is left, in its own words, needing "more arguments than I have space to give". |
| [LIT-449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-449.md) | What we talk to when we talk to language models | Chalmers (2026), Inquiry, DOI 10.1080/0020174X.2026.2727582; circulated earlier as PhilArchive preprint CHAWWT-8. Unread. By its abstract it asks who or what our interlocutor is when we talk to an LLM: how to characterise it in terms of mental states; what kind of system it is in the philosophy of computation ("a model, an instance, a thread, or a persona?"); what personal identity comes to for such interlocutors; and what follows for AI welfare and moral status. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-02 from Crossref, OpenAlex (which carries the abstract of the published version) and the author's papers page, not read: tandfonline.com, philpapers.org and philarchive.org returned 403 to every article and PDF URL, the Internet Archive was offline, and no other repository copy was found. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md) | Against Narrativity | Strawson (2004), Ratio 17(4):428–452. Rejects both the psychological Narrativity thesis (people do experience their lives as a story) and the ethical one (they should, to be full persons), naming Sacks, Bruner, Dennett, Taylor, MacIntyre and Schechtman. Distinguishes Diachronic self-experience (the self I am now was there in the past) from Episodic (it was not, though the human being was), and splits Narrativity into form-finding, story-telling and revision, with only story-telling sufficient. Episodics are normal and can live well; self-narration risks falsifying the self it describes. Argued from the author's own case. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-383](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-383.md)), in the published typeset text; worth reading as the standard objection to narrative accounts of the self, and for its distinctions: Episodic versus Diachronic self-experience, and form-finding, story-telling and revision as separable parts of "Narrativity". Read it as a report of a temperament argued from the author's own case and literary examples. Its empirical claims (a genetic "individual difference variable", the spread across cultures) are asserted, not shown, and its central metaphysical claim, that the remoter past did not happen to "me*", is stated rather than argued. |
| [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md) | Personal Identity | Olson (2002, rev. 2023), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Separates seven questions (characterization, personhood, persistence, evidence, population, personal ontology, what matters) and then takes up persistence. Three answers: psychological continuity (the majority view, repaired from Locke's memory criterion via causal dependence), brute-physical continuity (animalism), and anticriterialism. Fission forces the psychological view into multiple occupancy or a non-branching clause, which makes identity not what matters. The too-many-thinkers objection says that if we are not our animals there are two thinkers in every chair. Temporal-parts ontology may leave it indeterminate what we are. Avoids the word "self". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md)); worth reading as the standard map of the analytic personal-identity debate, written by the leading animalist. It separates seven questions that are usually run together, then works the persistence question through psychological-continuity, brute-physical and anticriterialist answers, fission and the too-many-thinkers objection. It is a survey with a side: §§6–7 put the case for animalism more fully than the case against it, and the entry sets the word "self" aside, so the narrative and minimal selves are outside it. |
| [LIT-464](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-464.md) | Of Identity and Diversity | Locke (1694), Essay II.xxvii, added in the second edition. Identity is relative to the idea the name stands for: the same mass is the same particles, the same oak or horse or man is the same continued life, and the same person is the same consciousness. A person is "a thinking intelligent being" that "can consider itself as itself", and personal identity reaches "as far as this consciousness can be extended backwards to any past action or thought". It is independent of substance, material or immaterial: the prince's consciousness in the cobbler's body is the same person but not the same man. "Person" is "a forensic term", grounding reward and punishment. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-385](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-385.md)), in the Wikisource transcription of the 1853 Troutman & Hayes reprint of the sixth-edition text, compared word by word with Project Gutenberg's; worth reading as the founding text of the psychological account of personal identity and the source of the record's whole line on what a person is. It separates the same substance, the same man and the same person, puts the person in "consciousness" extended back to past actions, and calls "person" a "forensic term". Its cases, the prince and the cobbler, the day-man and the night-man, the severed little finger, are argued from intuition, and its key relation, "the same consciousness", is never defined. |
| [LIT-465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-465.md) | Simulacra as Conscious Exotica | Shanahan (2024), Inquiry 69(6):2982–3010, from arXiv:2402.12422. After Wittgenstein, consciousness words mean only what is public, so the question for an exotic entity is whether we could "engineer an encounter" with it in a shared world and what a society-wide conversation would then say. Disembodied chat agents are not even candidates; virtually embodied LLM agents could be. Tool use and memory make belief talk increasingly literal, but a chat agent has no "self worth preserving", and a role player has no "person behind the mask": its identity is a shifting distribution of roles. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-382](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-382.md)) in the arXiv v2 preprint (July 2024), not the Inquiry version of record, which returned 403; worth reading as the Wittgensteinian alternative to the evidential debate about AI consciousness. It replaces "is it conscious?" with "could we engineer an encounter with it, and how would our language adapt?", and so counts disembodied chat agents as not even candidates. On the self it is brief and pointed: a chat agent has "nothing that would qualify as a self worth preserving", lacking body, personal history and autobiographical memory, and a role-playing agent has no "person behind the mask"; its identity, "insofar as that notion even made sense", is the shifting distribution of roles. It argues by method and scenario, not evidence, and says so. |
| [LIT-468](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-468.md) | The Constitution of Selves | Schechtman (1996), Cornell University Press. Separates the reidentification question (is this the same person?) from the characterization question (which actions, experiences and traits are this person's own?), and argues against analytic philosophy's attention to the first at the expense of the second. Chapters 1–3 take up reidentification; chapters 4–6 give the narrative self-constitution view, on which, as Strawson quotes it, a person "creates his identity [only] by forming an autobiographical narrative". The source of the term "characterization question" in the SEP map. Unread: registered from the description and the contents. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, the Library of Congress record and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Cornell/De Gruyter eBook is sold, not open, and the Internet Archive copy is for print-disabled users only. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-469](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-469.md) | Reasons and Persons | Parfit (1984), Clarendon Press; DOI-10.1093/019824908X.001.0001 is the 1986 reprint online. Four loosely connected parts, per the author's abstract: self-defeating theories of rationality and morality; what one person can rationally want at different times, and attitudes to time; personal identity, where "most of us … have certain beliefs about this subject that are false, but hard to give up"; and obligations to future generations, with the non-identity problem and the Repugnant Conclusion. By the chapter abstracts, Part III defends a reductionist view on which identity is not what matters and draws consequences for self-interest and distributive justice. Unread. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, its chapter abstracts and the table of contents; the book is in copyright and no lawful full text was reachable (the Internet Archive copies are lending-only and were not opened), so it is unread and no NOTE is filed. By its publisher's account, Part III argues that most of us hold false beliefs about personal identity, that psychological continuity and connectedness, not identity, is what matters, and that this should change our attitudes to our own future, to rationality and to morality. The record already leans on it at second hand: Birch's Relation R, Velleman's reading of Frankfurt and the identity-and-ethics survey all cite it. |
| [LIT-477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-477.md) | Walking Together: A Paradigmatic Social Phenomenon | Gilbert (1990), DOI-10.1111/j.1475-4975.1990.tb00202.x, Midwest Studies in Philosophy 15: 1–14. Gilbert takes going for a walk together as the model case of acting together and of a social group. Two analyses built from shared personal goals are rejected, because they cannot explain the walkers' obligations and rights to appropriate behaviour. Her alternative is that the walkers must constitute the "plural subject" of a goal. Unread: filed from metadata and the abstract as search indexes give it. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata; no lawful full text was reachable (Wiley and PDC are paywalled, the author's SSRN posting and a public PDF at humanitiesmontana.org both sit behind bot challenges that returned 403, and the Wayback Machine copy of that PDF could not be fetched through this session's proxy), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the short canonical statement of Gilbert's plural-subject account, and the record's only reading of Gilbert is second-hand, through Tomasello's commentaries ([NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md)). |
| [LIT-480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-480.md) | Gender and Race: (What) Are They? (What) Do We Want Them To Be? | Haslanger (2000), Noûs 34(1):31–55. Distinguishes conceptual, descriptive and analytical answers to "what is gender/race?" and takes the analytical one: define the terms for what a feminist antiracist theory needs. S is a woman iff S is regularly observed or imagined to have bodily features presumed to indicate a female's reproductive role, this marks S in the dominant ideology for subordinate positions, and that plays a role in S's subordination; men and racialized groups are defined in parallel, ethnicity and gender in general as the non-hierarchical genus. Stipulative by design; no evidence offered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-394](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-394.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of ameliorative ("analytical") social ontology and of gender and race as hierarchical social positions. It is short and explicit about its method: it defines woman, man and racialized group for the purposes of a feminist and antiracist theory, says so, and accepts the consequences (non-oppressed females are not women in its sense, and the goal is a world with none). Read it for the three-way distinction between conceptual, descriptive and analytical projects and for the definitional schema (marked by assumed bodily features, positioned by a dominant ideology, subordinated or privileged as a result), not for evidence: its "matters of established fact" about race are asserted without citation, and its definitions are stipulated, not discovered. |
| [LIT-483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-483.md) v2 | Groups as Agents | Tollefsen (2015), Polity. Per its publisher, a survey of whether groups can literally intend, whether there is a collective mind, and whether groups should be held morally responsible, arguing "the unorthodox view that certain groups should, indeed, be treated as agents and deserve to be held morally accountable". Chapters on group belief, intention, agency, cognition, interpreting groups and the moral responsibility of groups. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in print with Polity, licensed as an e-book, and no author-posted draft was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is a short introduction to group belief, intention, agency, cognition and responsibility that, per its publisher, argues "certain groups should, indeed, be treated as agents and deserve to be held morally accountable"; which groups, and on what view of agency, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-488.md) | Shared Agency: A Planning Theory of Acting Together | Bratman (2014), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199897933.001.0001. The planning structures that organise an individual's agency over time are also at the core of small-scale shared agency. A shared intention is constructed from each participant's intention that "we J", by way of each other's intentions and meshing subplans, with persistence interdependence and common knowledge. These conditions are offered as sufficient, not necessary. No group subject and no new primitive is needed: the account is reductive "in spirit", against Gilbert and Searle. Unread: filed from the chapter list and the author's précis. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata, the chapter list and the author's open-access précis; no lawful full text of the book was reachable (Oxford Academic is paywalled, and Bratman has not posted the book or draft chapters), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the developed statement of the reductive, planning-theory account of shared agency, and the précis, read in full, says plainly where it parts from Gilbert and Searle. |
| [LIT-493](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-493.md) | The Grammar of Society: The Nature and Dynamics of Social Norms | Bicchieri (2006; print December 2005), DOI-10.1017/CBO9780511616037. Per its publisher, an integrated account, drawing on social psychology, experimental economics and evolutionary game theory, of how social norms such as fairness, cooperation and reciprocity emerge, why and when people follow them, when they attend to the relevant norm, why inefficient norms survive, and how psychological dispositions can lead to fairness norms like ours. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. Cambridge Core is paywalled. The author's own copy of chapter 1 on her University of Pennsylvania pages and the publisher's excerpt at assets.cambridge.org both failed (HTTP 403; connection reset), and the Internet Archive has no copy. It is the standard equilibrium-and-expectations account of social norms; what its definition of a norm says was not seen. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-564.md) | The Sources of Normativity | Korsgaard (1992), Tanner Lectures at Clare Hall, Cambridge. The "normative question" asks what justifies morality's claims on us. Voluntarism, realism and reflective endorsement each fail alone. The answer is autonomy: because human consciousness is reflective, we need reasons, and so need a "conception of your practical identity" that makes us "a law to yourself". Obligation is "the reflective rejection of a threat to your identity". Valuing any identity commits us to valuing our humanity, and reasons are public, so others can obligate us. "Autonomy is the source of obligation." | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-465](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-465.md)), as the read substitute for the book The Sources of Normativity (1996, [LIT-599](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-599.md)), which is its "longer version" with commentaries and a reply. Worth reading as Korsgaard's own first statement of practical identity and of the claim that "autonomy is the source of obligation". The reflective structure of human consciousness means we must act for reasons and so must have "a conception of your practical identity", "a description under which you value yourself"; reasons express that identity and obligations "spring from what that identity forbids". Valuing any practical identity commits one to valuing one's humanity, and the publicity of reasons commits one to others. The lectures concede that the argument is "sketchy, and sketchily argued". |
| [LIT-594](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-594.md) | The Ethics of Authenticity | Taylor (1991), Harvard University Press, 142 pp.; first published in Canada the same year by Anansi as The Malaise of Modernity, an extended version of the 1991 CBC Massey Lectures. Unread. As commonly summarized (no publisher's description was reachable), it argues that the modern ideal of authenticity, being true to oneself, is a genuine moral ideal rather than mere narcissism or relativism, and that it is degraded when it is cut off from shared "horizons of significance" and from the dialogical way identities are formed. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from catalogue records, not read. No lawful full text was found: the book is in print with Harvard University Press, the Internet Archive copy (ethicsofauthenti00tayl, the 1992 printing) is an access-restricted lending copy, the publisher's digital edition at De Gruyter returned an empty bot-check response, and the full-text copies a web search turns up are file-sharing uploads, which were not opened. The book is about 140 pages, so a human reader with a library copy can read it in an afternoon; that reading would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-597](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-597.md) | Self-Constitution: Agency, Identity, and Integrity | Korsgaard (2009), Oxford University Press, from her 2002 Locke Lectures. The argument is that we constitute ourselves as agents, and as the particular agents we are, by choosing under the constitutive principles of action, the categorical and hypothetical imperatives. On Plato's "constitutional model", good action is action that issues from a unified soul. The chapters run from agency and identity to "How to be a Person". Unread: registered from the contents; the account is read in [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the Crossref records of the book and its ten chapters, not read: no lawful copy of the book could be reached. Its account is read first-hand in her short restatement "The Normative Constitution of Agency" (2014, [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md), read in full), which extends it. Filed because it is the canonical citation for self-constitution. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied or the drafts are read, not on merit. |
| [LIT-599](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-599.md) | The Sources of Normativity | Korsgaard (1996), Cambridge University Press, ed. Onora O'Neill: the expanded Tanner Lectures (1992), with commentaries by G. A. Cohen, Raymond Geuss, Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams and Korsgaard's reply. The four lectures follow the 1992 sequence: the normative question, reflective endorsement, the authority of reflection, and the origin of value and the scope of obligation. | [LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md) v3 | Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | Fischer & Ravizza (1998), Cambridge University Press. Unread seed. The most influential reasons-responsiveness theory of moral responsibility. Responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control (the control that involves alternative possibilities), and Frankfurt-type cases show the two come apart. An agent has guidance control of an action when it issues from her own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism: regularly receptive to reasons, including moral ones, and at least weakly reactive to them. The mechanism is her own when she has taken responsibility for it, which makes responsibility historical. Guidance control so described is compatible with causal determinism, which is the position Fischer calls semicompatibilism. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, from Crossref's book and chapter records, the chapter openings Cambridge Core displays, the record's second-hand readings, the SEP entry Moral Responsibility ([LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md)) and Fischer's own summary in "Stories and the Meaning of Life" ([LIT-689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-689.md), read), not read. No lawful full text was found: the book is paywalled at Cambridge Core, and Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy (oa_status closed, no repository holding). The shorter work the record's book rule asks for is the authors' own précis (Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 61(2), September 2000, first page 441, DOI 10.2307/2653660), also closed: JSTOR answered with a bot challenge, so I stopped there. Fischer's UC Riverside pages post no papers that could be reached, and the copies of the précis in two third-party collections of his papers (andrewmbailey.com/jmf and its wixsite continuation) are not the author's, a publisher's or a repository's, so they were not opened. A web search also shows a PDF titled "Fischer Guidance control and RR" on a UNAM institute's site, whose search snippet is the book's series page; it is a course file with no statement of permission, so it was not opened either. A person with Cambridge Core or library access can supply the book (Cambridge UP, 1998, DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511814594); chapters 2, 3 and 8 (pp. 28–91 and 207–239) are the parts to read first, and the short précis is the quickest way to an Active reading. Update 2026-10-05: the précis is now read (LIT-728), with chapter 1 to p. 19 from the publisher's preview. |
| [LIT-685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-685.md) v2 | Freedom Within Reason | Wolf (1990), Oxford University Press. Unread seed. The book-length Reason View: free will is "the freedom to be good, or the freedom to do the right thing for the right reasons" (publisher's abstract). It sets up the dilemma of autonomy, argues that the Real Self View (Hume, Frankfurt, Watson, Taylor) and the Autonomy View both fail, states the Reason View, defends its notion of ability against determinism, and asks what the True and the Good must be for the view to hold. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, from Crossref's book and chapter records (whose abstracts are each chapter's opening paragraph), the SEP entry the record holds and an MIT lecture handout, not read. No lawful full text was found: the book is paywalled at Oxford Academic, Unpaywall lists no open copy (oa_status closed), and no author or repository deposit turned up. The article is paywalled at Springer, whose page answered a plain request with a script challenge, so I stopped there; Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no open copy (oa_status closed), and the one repository location OpenAlex gives (a Georgetown handle, 10822/792792) does not resolve. | [LIT-687](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-687.md) v3 | Responsiveness and Moral Responsibility | Fischer (1987/88), in Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (CUP), pp. 81–106; read in its My Way reprint. Frankfurt-type cases show responsibility does not need the ability to do otherwise, so the mechanism that actually issues in action, not the agent, must be reasons-responsive, and weak responsiveness suffices. Responsibility is historical and compatible with determinism (semicompatibilism). | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-579](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-579.md)): in full, in the reprint in Fischer's My Way (OUP 2006), from Andrew M. Bailey's collection of Fischer's papers, used on the owner's instruction. Worth reading as the first statement of mechanism-based reasons-responsiveness. Frankfurt-type cases move the requirement from the agent to the mechanism that actually issues in the action; weak responsiveness is held sufficient; the result is named semicompatibilism. | [LIT-688](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-688.md) v2 | Asymmetrical Freedom | Wolf (1980), The Journal of Philosophy 77(3):151–166. Unread. By the SEP's report it is the origin of the Reason View's asymmetry: an agent who acts in accord with the True and the Good is praiseworthy even if psychologically determined so that she could not have done otherwise, but one who acts against it is blameworthy only if she could have done otherwise. Blame therefore needs regulative control and praise needs only guidance control, and Wolf answers the threat from determinism by denying that physical determination entails psychological determination. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref, the record's own second-hand readings and the SEP entry it already holds, not read. No lawful full text was found. The article is paywalled at JSTOR (stable 2025667) and the Philosophy Documentation Center, and JSTOR's free Early Journal Content stops long before 1980. Unpaywall lists no open copy (oa_status closed). The author's UNC faculty page posts no papers. PhilPapers (WOLAF) answered with a bot challenge, so I stopped there. The PDFs a web search turns up are a JSTOR download re-posted on an unrelated Squarespace site, a syllabus-collection upload on Weebly, and Scribd and Course Hero uploads; none is the author's, a publisher's or an institutional repository's, so none was opened. A person with JSTOR or PDCnet access can supply the 16-page PDF (Journal of Philosophy 77(3), pp. 151–166, DOI 10.2307/2025667); a reading of it would move this to Active and is the text the asymmetry THEORY candidate needs. |
| [LIT-689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-689.md) | Stories and the Meaning of Life | Fischer (2009), Philosophic Exchange 39(1), pp. 3–15. Section I sketches his framework for moral responsibility: guidance control, not regulative control, is the freedom-relevant condition; it consists in acting from one's own, moderately reasons-responsive mechanism; responsibility is historical and compatible with causal determinism; and the moral of Frankfurt-style cases is that it depends on how the actual sequence unfolds. The paper's thesis is that the value of acting freely is the value of artistic self-expression: free action makes a life a story with narrative value, though the life is judged mainly by moral and prudential standards. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-547](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-547.md)); worth reading as the only first-hand, lawful statement by Fischer that the record holds of his framework for moral responsibility: guidance control, not regulative control, is the freedom-relevant condition; guidance control is mechanism ownership plus moderate reasons-responsiveness; responsibility is historical and compatible with causal determinism; and the moral of Frankfurt-style cases is that responsibility depends on the actual sequence. Its own thesis is that the value of acting freely is the value of artistic self-expression, which gives a life narrative value. It lists the framework's elements without arguing for them. |
| [LIT-690](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-690.md) v2 | Sanity and the Metaphysics of Responsibility | Wolf (1987/88), in Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (CUP), pp. 46–62. Unread. By second-hand reports it argues that the "deep self" views of Frankfurt, Watson and Taylor, on which an agent is responsible when her actions flow from desires and values she identifies with, are insufficient. JoJo, raised by a vicious dictator, identifies wholly with the values he inherits yet is not responsible, because his upbringing leaves him unable to see right from wrong. What must be added is sanity: the ability to know and appreciate what one is doing and that it is right or wrong. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Cambridge's chapter record and opening extract, the record's second-hand readings and an MIT lecture handout about the essay, not read. No lawful full text was found. The chapter is paywalled at Cambridge Core (the page shows only the opening paragraph). Unpaywall lists no open copy (oa_status closed). The author's UNC faculty page posts no papers, and PhilPapers (WOLSAT) answered with a bot challenge, so I stopped there. The PDFs a web search turns up are an anthology reprint re-posted on an unrelated Squarespace site and Scribd and Course Hero uploads; none is the author's, a publisher's or an institutional repository's, so none was opened. A person with library access to Schoeman (ed.), Responsibility, Character, and the Emotions (Cambridge UP, chapter 3, pp. 46–62, DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511625411.003), or to any reprint (it is widely anthologised, including in Watson's Free Will), can supply the 17 pages; a reading of them would move this to Active and is the first-hand text the Reason View THEORY candidate needs. |
| [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md) | Moral Responsibility | Talbert (2019; revised 2024), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. A survey of moral responsibility: its relation to free will and determinism, forward-looking, Strawsonian and reasons-responsiveness accounts, the attributability/accountability distinction that grew from Wolf and Watson, the moral competence condition (Wolf's JoJo), conversational views, standing to blame, outcomes, skepticism, moral luck, ultimate responsibility, manipulation and the epistemic condition. Its §2.3 is a page-referenced summary of Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-548](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-548.md)); worth reading as the record's map of moral responsibility apart from the free-will question, and as its most exact second-hand source for two accounts the record cannot read first-hand: Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control (§2.3, with page references to the 1998 book) and Wolf's critique of Real Self views and her moral-competence condition, including the JoJo case (§§3.1.1, 3.2). It reports Wolf's praise/blame asymmetry only in one sentence of its preamble. |
| [LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Frankfurt (1971), The Journal of Philosophy 68(1):5–20. What is essential to a person is the structure of the will. A person's will is the effective first-order desire, the one that moves him "all the way to action" (p. 8). A second-order volition is wanting a desire to be one's will; persons have them, and wantons, who "do not care" about their wills, do not (pp. 10–11). Forming one is identifying with one desire and withdrawing from another (p. 13). Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, "securing the conformity of his will to his second-order volitions" (p. 15), and a decisive identification "resounds" through all higher orders (p. 16). Moral responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts "of his own free will" (pp. 18–20). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md)); worth reading as the source of the hierarchical account of the will, which the record has so far held only second-hand: first- and second-order desires, the will as the effective desire, second-order volitions, wantons and persons, freedom of the will as having the will one wants, decisive identification that "resounds" through higher orders, and a responsibility that needs neither a free will nor alternatives. Read it knowing that it is short and programmatic, that identification is stated, not analysed, and that it already contains both the decisive commitment (p. 16) and the acceptance of an addict made by another (n. 10), which the record's surveys date later. |
| [LIT-693](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-693.md) | The Importance of What We Care About: Philosophical Essays | Frankfurt (1988), Cambridge University Press: thirteen essays from 1969 to 1988, twelve reprinted "with minor stylistic changes" and "Rationality and the Unthinkable" new. Not read as a book. Its preface, read in the publisher's preview, says the essays' considerations are "primarily structural rather than historical", that volition rather than reason is the faculty they explore, and that necessity is "in certain respects essential" to autonomy. The record cites its pagination as IWWCA. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-04 as a seed, from Crossref and from Cambridge's publisher preview of the book (front matter, contents, sources, the three-page preface and reprint pp. 1–9 of chapter 1), not read as a book. The book is sold at Cambridge Core and Unpaywall lists no open copy. Its essays are filed one by one where they matter: chapters 1 and 2 ([LIT-694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-694.md), [LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md)) were read in full from their journal versions, and chapters 7 and 12 ([LIT-686](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-686.md), [LIT-575](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-575.md)) are Deferred. The seed is kept because the record cites the book's pagination ("IWWCA") throughout and because its preface states Frankfurt's method first-hand. A person with library access can supply the remaining essays; chapters 5, 8 and 12 are the ones the record's theories lean on. |
| [LIT-694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-694.md) | Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility | Frankfurt (1969), The Journal of Philosophy 66(23):829–839. The principle of alternate possibilities (PAP), "a person is morally responsible for what he has done only if he could have done otherwise", is false. Coercion excuses only when the agent acts because of it (§§II– III). Black, ready to make Jones4 act as he wants and never needing to, shows that circumstances can make an action unavoidable without playing any role in bringing it about (§IV); such a fact "does not help in any way to understand" the action and cannot excuse it (§V). PAP should be replaced by: not responsible "if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise", which "does not appear to conflict" with compatibilism (pp. 838–839). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-546](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-546.md)); worth reading as the origin of Frankfurt-style cases and the shortest first-hand statement of the argument against the principle of alternate possibilities: a fact that makes an action unavoidable but plays no role in bringing it about cannot excuse, so PAP should give way to "a person is not morally responsible for what he has done if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise" (p. 838). Read it knowing that its case is schematic (Black, Jones4 and "a certain action"; the voting and shooting versions in the record's surveys are later retellings), that its prior sign is in a footnote, and that it leaves "could have done otherwise" and "morally responsible" unanalysed on purpose (n. 1). |
| [LIT-698](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-698.md) | Collective Guilt | Isaacs (2011), ch. 3 of Moral Responsibility in Collective Contexts (OUP), pp. 71–94. Unread. By a summary of its abstract, it takes collective guilt to be blameworthy collective moral responsibility, a feature of collective agents that does not distribute to members; separates being guilty, believing oneself guilty and feeling guilty, and personal, membership and collective guilt; and, engaging Gilbert, concludes that collectives may be guilty without having guilt feelings. The review in NDPR confirms the non-distribution claim (pp. 81–83). | Deferred — filed 2026-10-04, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The work the owner means is chapter 3, "Collective Guilt", of Isaacs's Moral Responsibility in Collective Contexts (OUP, 2011); no Monist paper of that title exists. The book is paywalled, and none of Isaacs's shorter papers on collective responsibility (Midwest Studies 2014, New Criminal Law Review 2013) has an open copy. What is said here comes from Matt King's review in Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews (read in full) and from a search-service summary of the chapter abstract (unverified). A person with the book could supply the chapter; a reading would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-701](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-701.md) | Collective Guilt and Collective Guilt Feelings | Gilbert (2002), The Journal of Ethics 6(2):115–143. Unread. As read sources report it: it distinguishes personal, membership and collective guilt feelings, and defines collective guilt feelings by joint commitment, so that for us collectively to feel guilt over our action is for us to be jointly committed to feel guilt as a body. A plural subject can thus be in a collective emotion, and since emotions are separable from feelings, such emotions need no phenomenology of their own. Reprinted in Gilbert's Joint Commitment (2013), ch. 11. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-04, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. Springer and the OUP reprint are paywalled, Unpaywall finds no open copy, and the PhilArchive record (GILCGA) and SSRN abstract 1071254 both answered automated requests with a bot challenge or a block, which I did not try to get past. What the record says of it comes from Huebner's read paper, which quotes it with page references, and is labelled second-hand. A person with PhilArchive or library access could supply the text; a reading would move this to Active and should test Huebner's charge that a plural subject's emotion reduces to individual commitments. |
| [LIT-728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-728.md) | Précis of Responsibility and Control: A Theory of Moral Responsibility | Fischer & Ravizza (2000), Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 61(2):441–445. Moral responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control over alternatives. Guidance control is acting from a mechanism that is one's own, because one has taken responsibility for it, and that is moderately reasons-responsive: regularly receptive to reasons, some of them moral, and at least weakly reactive. The view is historical and compatible with causal determinism. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-575](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-575.md)): in full, from Andrew M. Bailey's collection of Fischer's papers, used on the owner's instruction. Worth reading as the authors' own five-page statement of the account of Responsibility and Control ([LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md)). It says moral responsibility requires only guidance control, which has two parts: the agent's ownership of the mechanism that issues in the action, acquired by taking responsibility for it, and that mechanism's moderate reasons-responsiveness. It summarises and does not argue; the arguments are in the unread chapters. |
